23.0.s.en: 1. A prayer for the sanctification of the senses and the enjoyment of wisdom

23.0.0.en: 1 O Lord, Father, Master of my life, do not abandon me to the counsel of my lips, and do not let me fall by them. 2 Who will set scourges over my thoughts and the discipline of wisdom over my heart, so that my follies are not spared and my sins are not overlooked? 3 Lest my follies be multiplied and my sins abound, and I fall before my adversaries and my enemy rejoice over me. 4 O Lord, Father, God of my life, do not abandon me to the counsel of my lips. 5 Do not let me lift my eyes in pride, and turn desire away from me. 6 Let not the desire of the belly nor fornication take possession of me, and do not give me over to an impudent soul.

23.0.1.en: O Lord, Father and Master of my life, do not abandon me to their counsel (my tongue and my lips), and do not let me fall because of them [1].

23.0.2.en: To whom do we pray? To the Lord, the Father and Master of my life; I have the boldness of sonship and the confidence that He gives me life instead of death.

23.0.3.en: And what do I ask? I entrust no one but the Father of my life to strike my thoughts with scourges!

23.0.4.en: I confess my sins, especially the sins of arrogance, evil desire and gluttony.

23.0.5.en: A person often feels that the commandments concerning the sanctification of the senses, the thought and the heart are higher than his spiritual stature; indeed it seems impossible for a person to fulfill these commandments while he has no authority over his senses, and indeed over his whole inner man. At the same time it befits us to realize God's love, for in the full freedom of our will we ask Him to sanctify our free will and to grant us longing together with zeal for holiness. No one is able to control his senses and sanctify them, therefore he must cry out to God, who alone is able to sanctify the lips and the thoughts and the mind and the eyes and all the desires, so that he does not fall before his adversaries, that is, the devil and his angels.

23.0.6.en: The prayer for wisdom in this chapter corresponds to a prayer of St. Ephrem the Syrian, which some Orthodox churches use in the Great Lent:

23.0.7.en: v My Lord and Leader of my life, take from me the spirit of laziness and faintheartedness, and the desire for power, and idle talk, but give to Your servant instead of these the spirit of purity, humility, patience and love.

23.0.8.en: Yes, O Lord and King, grant me to see my own faults, and not to judge my brothers.

23.0.9.en: For You are blessed from generation to generation. Amen.

23.0.10.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian Ben Sira mixes wise sayings with prayer: "O Lord, Father, Master of my life, do not abandon me to the counsel of my lips, and do not let me fall by them" [1].

23.0.11.en: a. Turning back from evil: "Return to the Lord and forsake your sins. Pray before His face, and lessen your offenses" (see 17:25). "Flee from sin as from a serpent, for if you come near it, it will bite you" (see Sir 2:21).

23.0.12.en: b. Honoring parents: "He who honors his father will be gladdened by his children, and in the day of his prayer he will be heard... For kindness to a father will not be forgotten, and will help in atoning for your sins" (see Sir 4:3, 14). Honor your father with all your heart, and do not forget the pains of your mother in childbirth. Remember that you were born of them, and what can you repay them for what they have done for you? (see Sir 7:27-28)

23.0.13.en: c. Preparing for the meeting with God: "Before offering a prayer prepare yourself, and do not be like a man who tempts the Lord" (Sir 18:23).

23.0.14.en: d. Serving as pleases the Lord: "He who serves the Lord according to His good pleasure will be accepted, and his prayer will reach to the clouds" (see Sir 35:16).

23.0.15.en: e. Meekness and humility: "The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds, and he is not comforted until it reaches the Lord" (see 35:17). "The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor before the Lord" (see Sir 18:3). "The wisdom of the humble lifts up his head, and seats him among the great" (see Sir 11:1).

23.0.16.en: f. Rising early for prayer: "He sets his heart to rise early to the Lord who made him" (see Sir 39:5).

23.0.17.en: g. Not repeating words in vain (Mt 6:7): "Do not repeat words in your prayer" (see Sir 7:14).

23.0.18.en: In his prayer Ben Sira asked the Lord, the Father and Leader of his life, to protect him from his tongue, and that the Lord would refine his mind and his heart and keep him from falling into error.

23.0.19.en: Ben Sira calls the Lord the Father and Master of my life; with the boldness of sonship he speaks with the Lord as a father to him, while He is his Master and Creator.

23.1.0.en: Who will subject my thoughts to scourges, and my heart to the discipline of wisdom, so that it does not spare my faults, nor neglect me in my sins? [2]

23.1.1.en: He asked the "Father and Master" of his life to subject his thoughts and his heart to scourges, as though Ben Sira wished to present himself as an example before his disciples. For he is no better than they, since he has no authority over his thought and his heart, that is, over his inner man, but needs God, his Father and Teacher and Trainer and Refiner, to take hold of the scourge in order to straighten his inner depths. If the wise Sirach declares his need of scourges from the Lord to set him straight, how can any of his disciples think that he is able to avoid sins of thought and emotion by his own effort?!

23.1.2.en: v "Who will subject my thoughts to scourges, and my mind to the discipline of wisdom, so that he does not spare my faults, nor overlook my sins? [2] Note in particular: "Who will subject my thoughts to scourges?" So there are scourges which scourge thoughts. They are the scourges of God, for the Word (the Logos), when He leads the soul to realize how it has sinned, scourges it. He scourges the blessed man who suffers from the scourgings, because the words (of rebuke) touch him and he does not complain against the one who rebukes him. But there are some without feeling, of whom it is said: "You have scourged them, but they did not grieve" (Jer 5:3) [1].

23.1.3.en: v Let us see what was said about sinners: "I scourged them (with whips), yet they felt no pain" (Jer 5:3). Earthly whips, when we strike living bodies with them, cause pain to those who are struck, whether they wish it or not. But the scourges of God are not so, for some of those struck feel pain and others do not... The wretched are those who do not feel pain from the blows of God, and the happy are those who feel pain from these blows.

23.1.4.en: The Book of Wisdom says in this matter: "They were only pricked that they might remember Your words, and then were quickly saved, lest they fall into deep forgetfulness and be deprived of Your kindness." As it was said: "Who will set a whip over my thoughts, and the words of the wise upon my lips, lest they be lenient with me in my faults, and I perish because of my sins" (see Sir 23:2).

23.1.5.en: Look carefully at these words: "Who will set a whip over my thoughts?" So there are whips for striking thoughts. It is God's scourges that strike thoughts, for the Word "Logos", when He takes the soul aside and pushes it and presses upon it until its conscience is awakened to the faults it has committed, scourges it.

23.1.6.en: So He strikes the blessed (wise) man, who feels pain under the blow, because the words of God have affected his soul, and he did not cast these words aside with contempt because they shamed him. But there is a man of whom it can be said that he is without feeling; of him it is said: "I struck them, yet they did not grieve" [2].

23.2.0.en: Origen Lest my faults be multiplied and my sins increase, and I fall before my adversaries, and my enemy rejoice over me [3].

23.2.1.en: The scholar Origen distinguishes between the whips of the world and the scourges of God. The first are material whips that fall upon living bodies, and everyone feels their pain. But God's scourges, which are for discipline, are of another kind; they fall upon the thought, and some receive them and feel them and offer repentance and return to God, and become blessed. Others do not feel their pains and do not respond to God's call to return to Him; these are struck and do not feel pain (Jer 5:3).

23.2.2.en: v It is said of sinners: "I struck them, yet they did not grieve" (5:3). The perceptible whips of this world fall upon living bodies, whether those who are beaten accept them or refuse them, and they are painful (to all). But God's scourges are of a kind that causes pain to some, while others do not suffer from them.

23.2.3.en: Let us explain what it means not to suffer from them. Why do these people of evil natures not suffer from God's scourges, while those who feel pain from them are blessed? Wisdom says: "Who will subject my thoughts to scourges, and set the seal of prudence upon my lips, so that he does not spare my faults, and my faults do not lead me to destruction."

23.2.4.en: Let us pay attention to the words: "Who will subject my thoughts to scourges." So there are scourges that are particular to striking thoughts. They are God's scourges that strike the thought, where the Word is joined to the soul and leads it to the knowledge of its sins. He strikes the blessed soul, and it suffers, for the Word comes and pierces the soul in its depths... But of him who is dulled with regard to the blow it is said: "I struck them, yet they did not grieve" [3].

23.3.0.en: Origen O Lord, Father and God of my life, do not give me haughty eyes [4].

23.3.1.en: He asked Him to remove from him his haughty eyes, that is, looking to high matters that are above his spiritual stature.

23.4.0.en: But turn away evil desire from me [5]

23.4.1.en: He asked the Lord not to allow the desire of gluttony or fornication to possess him, and not to give him over to an impudent soul (Sir 23:1, 4-6, 13, 15). This prayer describes the character of the wise man. It is prayer in faith, that the believer may be formed in the image of Wisdom herself.

23.5.0.en: Do not allow gluttony or desires to rule over me, and do not give me over to an impudent soul [6].

23.5.1.en: St. Augustine sees that many of these requests appeared among the divine commandments. Here St. Augustine asks why Sirach offers these requests when he knows that they agree with the will of God and His commandments. He answers that it befits the believer to declare his personal desire, affirming that his will is that the will of God be done in him. As though he were saying: "Thy will be done" (Mt 6:10) [4].

23.5.2.en: In St. Augustine's discourse[5] on grace and free will, he says that the followers of Pelagius think they know something important when they affirm that God commands nothing that He knows human beings are unable to practice. He comments saying: "Who does not know this?" and continues: But God gives commandments beyond our abilities, in order that we may know that we must ask Him, and He will give us the power to carry them out. So in faith we pray that we may fulfill the commandments. The saint presented many of the requests that the wise man (Ben Sira) asks, so that by grace we may practice what is beyond our strength.

23.5.3.en: St. Augustine sees that all the prayers in the Old Testament do not go beyond the Gospel prayer which our Lord Jesus taught us, and he gave many examples, among them some requests found in the Book of Sirach. The prayer found here: "Let not the desire of the belly nor fornication take possession of me" (see Sir 23:6) is nothing other than "Lead us not into temptation", and the request found in (Sir 36:4), which he translates "May You be sanctified among all men as You are sanctified among us", is nothing other than the request: "Hallowed be thy name" [6]

23.6.0.en: 7 O children, take hold of the discipline of the mouth; for he who keeps it is not caught by his lips. 8 For by them the sinner is trapped, and by them the slanderer and the proud stumble. 9 Do not accustom your mouth to swearing, 10 and do not become familiar with naming the Holy One. 11 For as a servant who is continually examined does not lack bruises, so he who continually swears and names is not purified. 12 A man who swears much is filled with iniquity, and the scourge does not depart from his house. 13 If he does not fulfill it, his sin is upon him, and if he treats it lightly, his sin is doubled. 14 And if he swears falsely he is not justified, and his house is filled with calamities. 15 There is also a manner of speech that is clothed with death. May it not be found in the inheritance of Jacob. 16 All these things are far from the godly; they do not wallow in sins. 17 Do not accustom your mouth to coarse speech, for that is not without sin. 18 Remember your father and your mother when you sit among the great, 19 lest you forget them before them, and the habit of associating with them make you foolish; then you would wish you had not been born of them, and curse the day of your birth. 20 He who is accustomed to words of abuse will not be disciplined all his days.

23.6.1.en: He concentrates on the faults of the tongue, and often enumerates them, as we have seen.

23.6.2.en: O my children, listen to the teaching of my mouth, for he who keeps it will not be defeated [7].

23.6.3.en: If Sirach asks for himself scourgings issuing from the hand of his Father, who is tender toward him and all-wise, in order that he may control his thoughts and his heart and his tongue, this tongue, which can destroy its owner and those around him, if it is sanctified, offers teaching according to the divine mind. Therefore he says to his disciples: "O my children, listen to the teaching of my mouth" [7]

23.7.0.en: Again he says: "There is a manner of speech that resembles death" [12]. For the tongue can be an instrument of righteousness for the sake of the Kingdom of God, bearing witness to the teaching of the Lord, or an instrument of iniquity that drives others to eternal death.

23.7.1.en: The sinner is trapped by his lips, and by them the abusive, proud man stumbles [8].

23.7.2.en: We are in need of a divine guard that keeps our lips from falling into sin.

23.7.3.en: v Moses taught you by the blood of the lamb which he sprinkled on the doors; it befits you to moisten your lips with the blood of the Son every day.

23.7.4.en: For the mouth is the door of man, which sends forth both praises and words, glory and abuse, of every kind.

23.7.5.en: David asked that a guard be set over him. Who is this one who stands as guard when he is asked, if not the Crucified?

23.7.6.en: David asked, saying: "Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth" (Ps 141:3). It is the Cross that guards the door of the mouth from Satan.

23.7.7.en: The Cross stood at the doors of the children of the people, and kept them from the slayer of the firstborn on the earth.

23.7.8.en: You too now, take the blood of the Son of God, and with your fingers trace the sign of the Cross upon your lips.

23.7.9.en: Make it a guard for your mouth, and be confident of its sure effectiveness, and then when the destroyer sees it he will not come near you.

23.7.10.en: If its symbol was able to stand at the door and guard them, how much more can He Himself guard the one who seeks Him?

23.7.11.en: Receive the blood from the divine cup upon your lips, and it will prove to you that it is a trustworthy guard of the door.

23.7.12.en: The doors of the people were sealed with the blood of the lamb, so seal your door with the blood of the side of the Son of God.

23.7.13.en: Dye your tongue and your lips and your mind with the blood of your Lord, and He will guard you from harm.

23.7.14.en: Seek every day this guard for your mouth and your lips; win him with tears, and he will keep you without sleeping.

23.7.15.en: The blood of the slain Christ is sprinkled upon the mouths of the people; Moses saw this and pictured it in the blood of the lamb [7].

23.7.16.en: St. Jacob of Serugh Do not accustom your mouth to vows, and do not become familiar with pronouncing the name of the Holy One [9].

23.7.17.en: For just as the servant who is continually beaten is not without bruises, so he who vows and pronounces the name of the Holy One continually is not cleansed from sin [10].

23.7.18.en: v "Do not accustom your mouth to swearing, nor let it become familiar with uttering the name of the Holy One" (see Sir 23:9). Why? "For as the servant who is still being beaten does not lack the marks of the blows, so he who swears" (see Sir 23:10).

23.7.19.en: See the discernment of this wise man. He did not say: "Do not accustom your mind but your mouth", because since this is entirely the work of the mouth, its remedy is easy. For this becomes a habit without intention, as for example there are many who enter the public baths merely by passing by their borders and crossing over them [8].

23.7.20.en: v It is impossible, entirely impossible, for a mouth that practices oath-taking not to commit false swearing. Therefore I ask all of you to abandon this deadly evil habit, so that you may receive another crown [9].

23.7.21.en: St. John Chrysostom The man who swears much is filled with iniquity, and calamity does not depart from his house.

23.7.22.en: If he sins, his sin is upon him. And if he treats the matter lightly, his sin is doubled.

23.7.23.en: And if he swears falsely he is not justified, and his house is filled with afflictions [11].

23.7.24.en: In the Old Testament a person was required to swear with dignity and truthfulness to bear witness to his faith in God, in contrast to the pagans who swear falsely by their gods (the idols). So the tongue that pronounces the name of the holy God, if it practices oath-taking often and without wisdom, swears falsely and its oath is counted as iniquity.

23.7.25.en: He warns us against haste in swearing by the name of the Holy One, lest it become a habit, and a person use it without wisdom and not be cleansed from sin. This habit drives a person to commit a doubled sin [11]: haste in swearing without prudence, and inability to fulfill what he swore to do (Lev 5:4; Num 30:2). Through this haste a person is exposed to blasphemy, whose penalty is death (Lev 24:15-16; Jn 10:33). It befits a person not to accustom himself to haste, not only in swearing by the name of the Holy One but even in the council of great men, lest he behave foolishly and be exposed to troubles, and wish he had not been born, and curse the day of his birth [14] (Job 3:3; Jer 20:14).

23.7.26.en: In the New Testament, as we have entered into spiritual maturity, the Lord commands us not to swear at all, but let our speech be yes, yes, and no, no. St. John Chrysostom explains this by saying that swearing is like the wind to the ship of anger; without it the ship cannot sail in a person's life. He says: [Lay down a law for a man who is very passionate never to swear, and there will be no need to teach him composure[10].] St. John Chrysostom considers not swearing to be the distinguishing mark of the Christian and his own language: [Let us receive this as a seal from heaven, so that we may be seen everywhere to be the flock of the King. Let us be known who we are by our mouth and our language][11].

23.7.27.en: v It befits a person never to swear, for it is written: "A man who swears much is filled with iniquity, and the scourge does not depart from his house" (see Sir 23:11). What was said about the scourge that does not leave his house is not to be understood of his earthly house, but of his soul (his soul), which is the temple of God [12].

23.7.28.en: Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles There is a manner of speech that resembles death. Would that it not be found in the inheritance of Jacob!

23.7.29.en: For the godly keep away from all these faults, and do not become entangled in sins [12].

23.7.30.en: Perhaps he means here speech of blasphemy against God, which deserves death and deprivation from the inheritance of Jacob, that is, from the Kingdom. He also means violent criticism that hurts feelings and spoils relationships, and may often develop into something worse than wounding feelings. It does not befit such a person to belong to the eternal inheritance.

23.8.0.en: Do not accustom your mouth to speak in indecent expressions, for this is sinful speech [13].

23.8.1.en: Our teacher James the Apostle calls us to control our mouths and our tongues, likening this to putting bridles in the mouths of horses that they may obey us, and we turn about their whole body (Jas 3:3). He also likens the tongue to the small rudder of the ship that moves the whole ship (Jas 3:4-6). He praises him who controls his tongue, saying: "If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body" (Jas 3:2).

23.8.2.en: Remember your father and your mother when you sit in the council of the great, lest you forget yourself before them, and by habit behave like a fool.

23.9.0.en: Then you would wish you had not been born, and curse the day of your birth [14].

23.9.1.en: v Hate greatness, for it is the fruit full of death.

23.9.2.en: For Adam ate of it in Eden, and it gave him death.

23.9.3.en: And by it Satan fell from the beginning. And by it the house of Adam fell from Paradise.

23.9.4.en: There is nothing with God so vile and hateful as the love of greatness and the haughtiness of pride.

23.10.0.en: St. Jacob of Serugh He who is accustomed to abusive words will not be disciplined all the days of his life [15].

23.10.1.en: Some think that abuse is to utter improper words against someone, but St. Basil sees that every word, even if it is not evil in itself, which distorts the image of others, directly or by implication, is abuse. St. Basil also warns us against insulting a person even with a general expression and with the intention of joking.

23.10.2.en: v Question: What is the abusive person?

23.10.3.en: Answer: Every word uttered with the intention of distorting the image of a person, even if the word itself does not seem to be abuse. This is clear from what the Gospel says of the Jews: "Then they reviled him, and said, Thou art his disciple" (Jn 9:28) [13].

23.10.4.en: v Question: What is the word "Raca" (Mt 5:22)?

23.10.5.en: Answer: It is a colloquial word of that nation for a slight, common insult, said by persons known to him without cost [14].

23.11.0.en: 21 There are two sorts of people who multiply sins, and a third sort that brings wrath. 22 The soul that burns like a blazing fire is not quenched until it is consumed. 23 And the man who commits fornication with the uncleanness of his flesh does not cease until he kindles the fire. 24 For to the fornicating man all bread is sweet; he does not tire until he is finished. 25 And the man who transgresses against his bed, saying in himself: "Who sees me? 26 Darkness is around me and the walls conceal me, and no one sees me; so what shall I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins." 27 He fears only the eyes of men, 28 and does not know that the eyes of the Lord are ten thousand times brighter than the sun; they see all the ways of men, and look into hidden places. 29 He knows all things before they are created; so also after they are finished. 30 So this man will be punished in the streets of the city, and where he does not expect, he will be seized, 31 and will be put to shame before all, because he did not understand the fear of the Lord. 32 So also the woman who leaves her husband and provides an heir for him from a stranger. 33 For first she disobeyed the law of the Most High, and second she betrayed her husband, and third she was defiled by adultery, and raised up offspring from a strange man. 34 This woman will be brought to the congregation, and the condition of her children will be examined. 35 Her children will not take root, and her branches will not bear fruit. 36 She will leave behind a cursed memory, and her disgrace will not be blotted out. 37 Then those who are left will know that there is nothing better than the fear of the Lord, and nothing sweeter than heeding the commandments of the Lord. 38 To follow God is great glory, and in being received by Him are length of days.

23.11.1.en: The gravest things about adultery are three:

23.11.2.en: a. Adultery is a blazing fire, which is not quenched except by the complete destruction of the person.

23.11.3.en: b. Despite the things about adultery from which the soul recoils, its pleasure lasts only minutes, offering sweetness to what is corrupt.

23.11.4.en: c. He who opens the door to adultery through negligence gives adultery a right of ownership over the heart and the mind and the emotions, and it clings to them, and the more negligent the person becomes, the harder it is to drive adultery out than it was. He who is negligent with desires and thoughts has his depths inflamed with a fire that is difficult to put out, and it remains aflame until the fire consumes him.

23.11.5.en: It seems that Ben Sira distinguishes three kinds of sins of men: 1. Adultery with an unmarried girl; the fire of this passion destroys a person (1 Cor 7:9). 2. Sexual relations between relatives, which the Law of Moses forbids marrying (Lev 18:6). This sin kindles the fire of divine wrath (Num 11:1). 3. Adultery with a married woman (9:9) is like one who eats bread that is pleasing to the soul (Prov 9:17; 30:20), and leads to death.

23.11.6.en: The one who commits adultery thinks that no one sees him, but God knows all the conduct of men (17:19-20), even if it seems hidden from everyone (Prov 5:21).

23.11.7.en: By meditating on the fate of the godly and the wicked, the believer is convinced that there is nothing better than life in the fear of the Lord and keeping His commandments (Eccl 12:13; Deut 10:12-13).

23.11.8.en: "The man who commits fornication with his body does not cease from this evil of his until the fire consumes him. To the fornicating man all food is sweet, and he does not rest until he dies. He who breaks his marriage vows, saying in himself: Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls hide me. And no one sees me; so what shall I fear? The Most High will not notice my sins. He fears the eyes of men, and does not know that the eyes of the Lord are ten thousand times brighter than the sun; they see all the ways of men, and penetrate into hidden ways" (see 23:16-19). "Do not gaze at the beauty of any man... for from garments comes the moth" (see 42:12-13).

23.11.9.en: There are two sorts of people who multiply sins, and a third sort that brings wrath [16].

23.11.10.en: The danger of not controlling the tongue, and also of falling into desires, appears in that both strike the whole society, because the relationships among the members of society are often based on dealing by the tongue, and on sex as the biological basis of marriage and the formation of the family, which is the pillar of society and the chief element in establishing the community.

23.11.11.en: Corruption of speech destroys trust among people, and corruption of sex destroys the family order on which all humanity rests and which gives it unity. If there is no control of sex, there is no control of the tongue either. Adultery is not only a sin against purity but also against justice, for adultery is a violation of the human covenant. When a person commits adultery he does not offend only against his family but also against society. The chief remedy for these sins is the enjoyment of the fear of the Lord.

23.11.12.en: The soul that burns like a blazing fire is not quenched until it is consumed.

23.11.13.en: And he who gives over his whole body to fornication does not stop until the fire burns him.

23.11.14.en: To the fornicating man all food is sweet, and he does not stop until he dies [17].

23.11.15.en: v Let us provide wives (for our sons) at an early age, so that the brides may receive their bodies pure and undefiled, and their love may be more ardent. He who is pure before marriage is all the more pure after marriage; and he who practices fornication before marriage practices it after. "To the fornicating man all food is sweet" (see Sir 23:17).

23.11.16.en: Crowns are usually placed on the heads of bridegrooms as a symbol of victory, indicating that they approach the marriage bed not defeated by pleasure. But if he is a captive of pleasure and has given himself to a harlot, why does he wear the crown while defeated?![15]

23.11.17.en: v It is a passion that has no limits. Again, those who take pleasure in fornication cannot cease from it. It is said: "To the fornicating man all food is sweet" (see Sir 23:17). He does not stop until he is devoured. For it is a passion![16]

23.11.18.en: St. John Chrysostom v He who thinks that he hides his crime is lost through an empty hope, for this is a false saying and there is no truth in it. And the false speech that sinners utter is hateful (see Sir 27:13). It produces not fruit but a burden. For the talk of the fool is like a load on the road (see Sir 21:17). And what is sin but a heavy load? It is heavy, carried by the fugitive in this life, where he is greatly weighed down by the heavy load of his crime. If he does not wish to fall under the burden, he must give heed to the Lord who says: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 11:28) [17].

23.11.19.en: St. Ambrose The man who transgresses against his marriage bed, saying in himself: "Who sees me?

23.11.20.en: Darkness is around me, and the walls of my house hide me. And no one sees me; so what shall I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins" [18].

23.11.21.en: v Let us always walk honestly, as in the day (Rom 13:12), and renounce the works of darkness. We know that the night has been appointed for the rest of the body, not for work and activities, therefore we spend the night in sleep in comfortable forgetfulness, and we do not spend it in feasting and drunkenness and revelry and immodesty. It befits us not to say: The darkness and the walls hide us, for the Most High observes us and sees us. Instead of this let us love the light and walking in the sunlight, and desire that our works be radiant in the presence of God [18].

23.11.22.en: v Every person who avoids the light loves the darkness, seeking to hide, although he cannot hide from God, who knows not only what actually happens, but even what is thought, whether in the depths of a place or in the minds of men. So the Book of Jesus son of Sirach also says: "Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls conceal me. And no one sees me; so what shall I fear?" (see Sir 23:18) [19].

23.11.23.en: St. Ambrose v He who seeks mere sexual pleasure turns his marriage into adultery. He forgets the words of the Teacher: "The man who breaks his marriage vows, saying in himself: Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls hide me. And no one sees me; so what shall I fear? The Most High will not notice my sins" (see Sir 23:18). Such a man is utterly wretched, for he fears only the eyes of men, and thinks that he is hidden from God. "He does not know what the Scripture tells him: that the eye of the Lord is brighter than the sun... they see all the ways of men, and penetrate into hidden ways" (see Sir 23:19). At another time the Teacher warns us through Isaiah: "Woe to you who make your counsel in secret, and say: Who sees us?" (Isa 29:15) LXX.

23.11.24.en: The light that the senses can see may pass and we do not notice it, but that which enlightens the mind cannot be ignored... May we not allow ourselves to be swallowed up by darkness by any means, for the light dwells in us, and the darkness cannot overcome it (see Jn 1:5). The night is turned to day by pure prudence.

23.11.25.en: Holy Scripture calls for a day by pure prudence. Holy Scripture calls the mind of the good man a lamp that cannot be put out (Wis 7:10). In fact, the very attempt to cover over what a person does is a sign that the person realizes he is committing a sin [20].

23.11.26.en: St. Clement of Alexandria The eyes of men are his fear, and he does not know that the eyes of the Lord are ten thousand times more radiant than the sun; they see all the ways of men, and observe even the hidden places [19].

23.11.27.en: v Such a person is utterly wretched, for he fears only that people will notice him, and thinks that he is hidden from God [21].

23.11.28.en: St. Clement of Alexandria In a letter that St. Ambrose sent to St. Irenaeus he affirmed that those who think that God does not see them because they practice evil in the darkness, and that the depths cover them, their hope is in vain, for God sees the hidden depths that cannot be fathomed; everything is exposed before Him before it happens.

23.11.29.en: He also made clear that the prophet Elijah chose to dwell in the mountains, and his disciple Elisha used to dwell in the upper room.

23.11.30.en: v Elijah and Elisha did not live in dwellings below the surface of the earth. One of them carried the dead son of the widow to the upper room where he was dwelling, and there he restored him to life (2 Kgs 17:22). The other had a chamber prepared for him in the upper room by the great Shunammite woman, as the Scripture testifies... What shall I say of Peter, who went up to the housetop at the sixth hour and learned the mystery of the baptism of the Gentiles (Acts 10:9)? On the other hand the criminal Absalom set up for himself a pillar in the king's valley, and he was thrown into a pit when he was killed (2 Kgs 18:7).

23.12.0.en: Thus the saints go up to the Lord, and the wicked go down into sin. The saints are on the mountains, and the criminals are in the valleys, for He is the God of the mountains and not the God of the valleys (1 Kgs 20:28) [22].

23.13.0.en: v Let us walk honestly, as in the day, and leave the works of darkness (Rom 13:12-13). We know that the night passes in sleep and forgetfulness so that the body may find rest. The night was not appointed for the practice of any work or any dealings. Let us not take part in parties and drunkenness... Let us not say: "The darkness and the walls cover us; who knows whether the Most High sees us" (see Sir 23:19). Let there be in us a love of the light and our appreciation of goodness, so that we may be like one who walks in the day, desiring that our works shine in the presence of God [23].

23.13.1.en: St. Ambrose He knows all things before the world was created, and the end of all things is also known to Him [20].

23.13.2.en: This adulterer will be punished in the streets of the city, and where he does not expect, he will be seized [21].

23.13.3.en: So also is the woman who leaves her husband and provides an heir for him from a stranger [22].

23.13.4.en: As for the adultery of the woman [22-27], her sin is three-sided:

23.13.5.en: a. Breaking the law of God (Deut 5:18; Ex 20:14).

23.13.7.en: c. Bearing children who are not from her husband.

23.13.8.en: According to the Mosaic Law the woman is stoned to death (Deut 22:22; Additions to Dan 13:36-41), and deprives herself of practicing motherhood and enjoying her grandchildren (Wis 3:16-19; 4:3-6). Instead of being honored after her death, her memory becomes a disgrace (Sir 41:5-9).

23.13.9.en: For first she disobeyed the law of the Most High, and second she sinned against her husband, and third she was defiled by adultery, and bore children by a strange man [23].

23.14.0.en: This woman will be brought to the council, and an investigation will be made into the matter of her children [24].

23.15.0.en: Her children will have no roots, and her branches will not bring forth fruit [25].

23.16.0.en: She will leave behind a cursed memory, and her disgrace will not be blotted out [26].

23.17.0.en: Then those who remain after her will know that there is nothing better than the fear of the Lord, and nothing sweeter than care for the commandments of the Lord [27].

23.17.1.en: v O you who love teaching and long to listen, receive once more the holy words, and delight yourselves with the honey of wisdom, for it is written: "Good words are a honeycomb, and their sweetness is the healing of the soul" (Prov 16:24) LXX. The work of the bee is very sweet and benefits the soul of man in many ways, but the divine, saving honey makes those in whom it settles skilled in every good work, and teaches them the ways of spiritual progress [24].

23.17.2.en: St. Cyril the Great v Do you love pleasure and delights? Look to the commandments of the Lord, for to the sound soul they are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb![25] It is the charm of the truth which the psalmist expressed, affirming it when he said: "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" The yoke of Christ is sweet, and its burden light in refreshing those who submit to it, but everything foreign to the teaching of the Gospel is heavy and wearisome (Mt 11:28-30) [26].

23.17.3.en: v Question: How can one who has become slack in the commandment regain his zeal and watchfulness?

23.17.4.en: Answer: By being convinced of the presence of the Lord God, who watches over all things everywhere, and by setting before his eyes the threat against the slack, and the hope of a great reward from God, who promised it through Paul the Apostle, saying: "Every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour" (1 Cor 3:8), and similar expressions which encourage zeal and patience in everyone for the glory of God [27].

23.17.5.en: v Question: How can a person fulfill the commandments of the Lord by an inner impulse and with zeal?

23.18.0.en: Answer: By nature, through the experience of what is sweet and beneficial, and the expectation of anything of this kind, an impulse and a longing for it is born in the soul. Therefore if one hates iniquity and abhors it (Ps 119:163), and is cleansed from every sin, then just as when the body loses appetite and the pleasure of food because of illness, so through the sickness of sin the soul suffers from dullness and aversion to the righteous judgments of God. And if one is fully convinced that God's commandment is eternal life (Jn 12:50), and that all the promises for those who keep them are true, then by this the impulse works in him, for it is said: "The judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold and very precious stones, sweeter also than honey and the dripping of the honeycomb. Moreover by them is thy servant warned, and in keeping of them there is great reward" (Ps 19:10-12) [28].

23.18.1.en: St. Basil the Great Inspired by Sirach 23

23.19.s.en: Have mercy on me, my Father, from my own counsel!

23.19.0.en: v To You I complain of myself, O Lord, Father and Master of my life.

23.19.1.en: Let Your will be done in my life, and let my negligent counsel be crucified.

23.19.2.en: Who can discipline my negligent thoughts and scourge them with whips but You?

23.19.3.en: I entrust no one to scourge my thoughts but You.

23.19.4.en: For You are a compassionate heavenly Father, almighty and knowing all my depths!

23.19.5.en: With Your firm scourges, full of love, shatter the arrogance of my haughty eyes.

23.19.6.en: To You alone belongs the authority to uproot my evil desires and gluttony, and all corruption, from their roots.

23.19.7.en: v Support me and set a strict guard to keep my tongue.

23.19.8.en: Do not allow a word of abuse or arrogance or haste in vows to issue from my mouth.

23.19.9.en: Do not allow my defiled mouth to be negligent and swear by Your name, O You who alone are Holy!

23.19.10.en: Words of blasphemy attack my mouth to occupy it, so that death may come upon me.

23.19.11.en: As a son of Yours, do not allow cheap, unseemly words to issue from my mouth!

23.19.12.en: v Extinguish the fires of desires lest they burn me and destroy me completely.

23.19.13.en: All souls, however corrupt, realize that desires are bad; their pleasure may last for minutes and the soul recoils from them.

23.19.14.en: But when they take hold of a person's heart and mind, they strike their roots into his depths, and reckon that they have established their kingdom in him...

23.19.15.en: Who can drive them from the seat of their throne?!

23.19.16.en: You alone, O Holy One, shine forth with Your righteousness, and the darkness of desires is dispelled!
